0e58bbfd54ae9e8b.text: How an ad gets its message across. An ad is a film text with a clear purpose — to sell, to warn, to change what you do — and a clear audience. Everything in it is a choice. Pictures. A close-up shows a face and a feeling. A wide shot shows the place. Bright colours feel fun; dark colours feel serious. Sound. Music tells you how to feel. A voice-over explains. A sudden sound effect makes you jump. Words. Text on screen, a catchy slogan, and a call to action: the thing they want you to do. Structure. Most ads follow a shape: a hook in the first few seconds, a build, the message, then the call to action. The makers think hard about the audience. An ad for teens might use humour, music and fast cuts. An ad for older people might be slower and calmer. To pull an ad apart, ask: What's it for? Who's it for? How do the pictures, sound and words help?

c1c7f7ca62a01548.text: Dumb Ways to Die. In November 2012, Metro Trains Melbourne released a safety campaign made by the ad agency McCann Melbourne. It didn't look like a safety ad at all. It was a cartoon music video called Dumb Ways to Die. Cute, colourful characters met silly ends to a catchy song. Only near the end did the real message arrive: some of the dumbest ways to die are around trains. Then came the call to action: be safe around trains. It spread around the world online, and people shared it because it was funny, not because it was a warning. In 2013 it won five Grand Prix awards at the Cannes Lions, one of the world's biggest advertising festivals. The makers knew their audience: young people who tune out serious safety messages. So they hid the message inside something people wanted to watch. Think about it. What was the purpose, and who was the audience? Why make a safety ad funny? When does the real message arrive, and why then?

9222b3a4321825c5.text: How an ad gets its message across. An advertisement is a film text constructed for a specific purpose — to sell, to warn, to change behaviour — and a specific audience. Nothing in it is accidental. Visuals. Shot types position the viewer: a close-up builds emotion, a wide shot establishes setting. Colour, lighting and editing pace set the tone. Sound. Music cues emotion, voice-over explains, and sound effects create surprise or tension. Language. On-screen text, a memorable slogan, and a call to action that tells the audience what to do. Structure. Most ads hook the viewer in the first few seconds, build interest, deliver the message, then close with the call to action. These choices depend on the audience. A campaign aimed at teenagers might use humour, music and rapid editing; one for older viewers might be slower and more direct. To analyse an ad, ask: What is its purpose? Who is the audience? How do visuals, sound, language and structure work together?

f21f274f1655ae68.text: Dumb Ways to Die. In November 2012, Metro Trains Melbourne launched a rail safety campaign made by the agency McCann Melbourne. It took an unexpected approach. Instead of scary warnings, it was a cartoon music video: Dumb Ways to Die. Colourful characters met absurd ends to a cheerful, catchy song. Only towards the end did the real subject appear — dangerous behaviour around trains — followed by the call to action: be safe around trains. The video spread internationally because audiences enjoyed it and chose to share it. In 2013 it won five Grand Prix awards at the Cannes Lions, a major world advertising festival. It was made for young people, who often ignore serious safety ads. By hiding the warning inside something fun, the makers turned viewers into people who spread the message. Think about it. What was the purpose, and who was the audience? Why make a safety ad funny? When does the real message arrive, and why then?
